tagline.text: The highest peak on Mindoro, a four-day trek on one of the toughest mountains in the Philippines

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱6,000–10,000 (4 days, 3 nights from Manila, per person in a team of five)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport, Manila (MNL; continue to Mindoro by land and ferry)

children.text: Mount Halcon is the highest peak on Mindoro at roughly 2,582–2,616 m, and it is known as one of the hardest mountains in the Philippines. The standard route is a 3.5- to 4-day climb from Lantuyan in Baco, and a licensed local guide and an advance permit are required.

Mount Halcon rises in Baco, Oriental Mindoro, and is the highest peak on the island of Mindoro. Sources give its height anywhere from 2,582 m to 2,616 m, and it has not been confirmed by an official survey. It is classed as a 9/9 major climb, the toughest grade in Philippine mountaineering, and is regarded as technically demanding because steep slopes, frequent rain, leeches, river crossings and a knife-edge ridge all come together.

This is not a mountain for casual visitors. A licensed local guide is required, and a permit must be obtained from the Baco tourism office. The climb usually takes about four days, and the Alangan Mangyan indigenous community lives at the foot of the mountain. The critically endangered Mindoro bleeding-heart pigeon lives in the forest, and the mountain is also known for the story that a Japanese WWII holdout hid here. It is too hard to be your first mountain, and you need experience on several well-known peaks beforehand. It is also an old challenge: an expedition led by the American botanist Elmer Merrill in 1906 is recorded as its first ascent.

The climbing window is stated as February 1 to May 31. Outside it, heavy rain makes the river rise and the trek dangerous. Permits are limited in number and reservations are required, so preparation starts months ahead, and the rules can change from year to year, so confirm the latest requirements with the Baco tourism office. Information differs slightly from review to review and guide to guide, so always check with the official office.

This guide aims less to encourage a climb than to tell you honestly about the preparation and the risks. Go with a mountaineering club or an experienced team, and attempt it only after thoroughly checking your equipment and fitness and preparing for emergencies. On Halcon, returning safely matters more than reaching the summit.

The summit is an ultramafic rock area, and reviews say that on a clear day the view extends toward Mount Banahaw. Clouds are frequent, so the view takes some luck. To see the sunrise from the summit, you must set out from the summit camp very early, and a headlamp is essential.
This campsite at about 1,100 m is reached on the first day and is surrounded by peaks and waterfalls. It is where you check how you are feeling before the serious climbing begins.

You cross this river on the second day, and upstream there is clear water and small campsites. If rain falls for 12 hours or more, you may not be able to cross, so follow your guide's judgment. Before crossing, undo your pack's chest and hip straps so you can get out of the pack if you are swept away. Upstream there are pools of clear water that are nice to rest at while camping.
Beyond the forest line, a narrow ridge continues, with a wooden ladder section. Some say it does not feel frightening once you are there, but it is dangerous in wind and rain.
You pass the indigenous community around Lantuyan, and your guide can teach you greetings and cultural etiquette. Do not take photos without permission.

Leeches are reported to be very abundant, so leech socks, gaiters and insect repellent are essential. The misty mossy forest and the waterfalls are another sight on this mountain. Leech bites do not hurt, but the bleeding takes a long time to stop, so bring bandages. Wet leaf litter is slippery, and trekking poles help.
This is an area of high biodiversity, home to the critically endangered Mindoro bleeding-heart pigeon and rare insects. Do not collect wildlife or plants.

items.title: Classic four-day route
items.subtitle: From Lantuyan to the summit camp and back down

children.text: Travel from Manila to Batangas Port, take the ferry to Calapan, then take a chartered jeepney to Baco Municipal Hall. Finish the permit paperwork and orientation in the morning and stay near the Lantuyan trailhead.
Start from the Lantuyan trailhead and climb to Aplaya campsite (about
elevation). It is a relatively gentle stage, but there are many leeches.
Descend from Aplaya to the Dulangan River, cross it and rest at the riverside campsite. The steep descent and the crossing take a lot of energy.
Climb to the summit ridge and summit camp. After the knife-edge ridge, it takes more than another hour to reach the true summit.
See the sunrise from the summit, then descend to the Lantuyan trailhead. Discuss any change of schedule with your guide.

The schedule changes with the weather and your team's fitness. Some teams compress the four-day route into a three-day summit push, but it is much harder. Some sources give a guide ratio of about one guide per seven climbers, so check how many guides your team size needs. On the descent day your legs tire and slip easily, so stay focused until the last stretch.
Request a reservation from the Baco tourism office and confirm your group size and dates.
Prepare a medical certificate and either a basic mountaineering course certificate or proof of a previous major climb, and check your equipment.
Check the weather, river level and local news, and finalize your plan with your guide.
Documents and requirements can change, so always confirm the latest requirements at the official office.

items.title: From Manila to Baco by land and ferry

children.text: Take a bus from Manila to Batangas Port and a ferry to Calapan Port in Oriental Mindoro. One guide gives the total from Manila to Baco as about 6–8 hours.
From Calapan to Baco, use a chartered jeepney or van, and one guide puts a jeepney at about
per vehicle. If it is late, it is safer to stay a night in Calapan.
Ferry schedules and fares change often, so check the operator's notices before you leave.

items.title: From Baco to the Lantuyan trailhead

children.text: The permit must be obtained at the tourism office in Baco Municipal Hall and cannot be obtained at the trailhead.
The Lantuyan trailhead is described as about
45 minutes
by vehicle from the municipal hall.
Register your climb and emergency contacts at Baco Municipal Hall before you set out. Registration is essential for safety.
Bayanan is an alternate trailhead used in some traverse itineraries. The route is different, so discuss the choice with your guide.
The climbing window is stated as February 1 to May 31, and February–March is the most stable, while late May is unpredictable. It can rain even in the dry season, so waterproof all your gear.

In the rainy season, there is a serious risk of sudden floods that make the river impassable. In the past, people have died of hypothermia during typhoons, so do not climb outside the permitted window.

Even inside the permitted window, afternoon showers increase in April and May. In that case, move your day earlier so that you reach camp early in the afternoon and get less wet. Permits sell out fast around holidays and Holy Week, so lock in your dates early.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most stable period, and competition for permits is high.
Start early and check the river level often.
Heavy rain and crossing risks are too high, so do not climb.

You camp in tents on the mountain, and there is no lodging. It is safer to stay a night in Baco or Calapan the day before the climb. Baco has small guesthouses, but they are small and their names and rates change, so check recent reviews on a map app.

Preparing food is basically the team's job. Decide in advance whether to include the guide's and porter's meals, and many people set aside about ₱150–200 per day separately for the guide's food. Bring plenty of rice, canned food, energy snacks and electrolyte drinks. You will treat stream water, so you need a filter or purification tablets. There have been complaints that guides sometimes arrive without enough gear or food, so check beforehand.

After you return, it is common to rest in Calapan with a hot meal and a shower. The travel time is long, so returning to Manila on the day you come down is difficult, and we recommend a rest day. Start moving early the next morning, and check the ferry departure times at Calapan Port in advance. Do not forget to tell your family your schedule and your expected return date.
Permits are issued per person and the numbers are limited, so reserve 2–3 months ahead.
Prepare a medical certificate and a basic mountaineering course certificate (or proof of a previous major climb).
Waterproof everything with a pack cover and plastic bags. It rains even in the dry season.
Bring leech socks, gaiters and insect repellent, and undo your chest and hip straps before crossing the river.
Prepare for hypothermia by keeping warm clothes and a change of clothes dry.
Check beforehand that your guide has enough gear and food, and have the team provide what is missing.
In the Mangyan village, ask before taking photos and carry out all your trash.
Many stretches have no mobile signal, so carry an offline map and a satellite emergency device.
Keep your pack to around 15 kg and include spare socks, a headlamp, a power bank, first aid supplies and a water filter.

Halcon is among the most dangerous trekking routes in the Philippines. Above the summit camp there is no road access, so after an accident it can take 8–12 hours to carry someone down. Never go alone or without experience and preparation.
The Dulangan River becomes dangerous after 12 hours or more of rain. Sometimes it takes courage to turn back on your guide's judgment.
The knife-edge ridge is very dangerous in strong wind and in the rain. Always follow your guide's instructions.
Hypothermia is a leading cause of death even on tropical mountains. Change out of wet clothes right away.
Climbing without a permit or outside the permitted window is a violation of the rules, and rescue is difficult if an accident happens.
Rules and fees can change, so check the latest notices from the Baco tourism office.
Permits are issued per person and there is a daily limit, so you cannot get one on the spot. If you go without a reservation, you may come away empty-handed.
A resort on the north coast of Oriental Mindoro, a good place to unwind after a climb. It is connected by road from Calapan.
Puerto Galera's main beach, well suited to a recovery stay after the climb.
A diving site in the sea west of Mindoro. Consider it a separate trip if you have more time.
